title: Mother 'not told' about Tasers
subtitle: Riki Bagnell says she learned about the weapons' use a month after her son died
article: The Vancouver police department didn't disclose it had used high-voltage Tasers when a police detective phoned a mother in Prince Edward Island to inform her that her 44-year-old son had died while police were trying to arrest him.

The next-of-kin notification came two days after the June 23, 2004, death of cocaine-drugged Robert Wayne Bagnell, who was swearing and smashing things in a bathroom of the Granville Street hotel where he lived.
Riki Bagnell told a coroner's inquest Wednesday she was "in a state of shock" when police called, but "not totally surprised."
She said her son was a musician and artist, but had been "dabbling" with cocaine and heroin since age 18.
"As a mother of someone who lived that lifestyle, I always had nightmares about wondering where he was, and what he was doing," said Riki Bagnell, who sometimes didn't hear from her son for years.
She said Vancouver police Det. Rob Faoro said her son "died from a possible overdose," and that toxicology tests would probably confirm what had happened.
The mother had several more telephone conversations with Faoro, whom she credited with helping her get her son's body returned to P.E.I.
But not until July 23, 2004 -- exactly one month after her son's death -- did the mother learn that Vancouver police had zapped her son with an electrical charge.

She heard the news second-hand --not from a police source -- that a Taser might have been used. A Vancouver television station had reported that police had used Tasers while arresting Bagnell. A family friend in Vancouver phoned Ontario resident Patti Gillman, who is Riki Bagnell's daughter and Robert Bagnell's sister. Gillman woke up her mother that night at 1 a.m., urging her to listen to a Vancouver newscast on satellite TV.
"I was beside myself," the mother said. "I couldn't believe it."
Riki testified that she later asked Faoro: "If you were worried about a broken toilet or sink, why didn't you just wait until he had calmed down?"
According to the mother, the police detective replied: "That's a very good question."

That August -- after Bagnell's death and after the B.C. Police Commission ordered a review of the use of Tasers by police forces in B.C. -- Vancouver police issued a news release which offered an explanation.

"Just as they \[police\] were settling down to wait, the fire alarm in the building went off," the release stated. "There was a fire on the ground floor of the hotel. Smoke began to fill the building. The police could not stay there any longer, and they certainly could not leave Mr. Bagnell behind. The call to arrest Mr. Bagnell had now turned into a rescue."

Vancouver police Det. Sean Trowski, another homicide investigator assigned to investigate Bagnell's death -- told the inquest that two Vancouver police officers touched Bagnell with their Tasers while pulling him out of the washroom.

But Trowski, who arrived on the scene at about 12:50 a.m., wasn't immediately told that Tasers had been used. He confirmed that a hotel tenant was the first person to suggest a Taser might have been used. The police officers had already returned to their offices, where they were getting post-trauma counselling and had a chance to speak to a police union representative -- VPD policy when an officer is involved in a death while police are trying to arrest someone.
Ten days have been set aside for the inquest, which began Tuesday.
